batch: Key Takeaways re-sweep 2026-08-25 — survivals of earlier body corrections

edits.before: I-20 is the primary east-west freight artery through the South Carolina Midlands, carrying thousands of tractor-trailers daily through Lexington and Richland counties. South Carolina recorded 3,167 large truck crashes in 2024 with a 23% increase in fatal truck accidents. Explosive growth in distribution and logistics along the I-20 corridor in Lexington County is driving more truck volume onto roads shared with commuters. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.

Explosive growth in distribution and logistics along the I-20 corridor in Lexington County is driving more truck volume onto roads shared with commuters. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.

edits.before: I-526 (Mark Clark Expressway) connects the Port of Charleston's two major terminals and carries some of the heaviest commercial truck traffic in South Carolina. The I-26/I-526 interchange recorded 354 collisions over 5 years. Charleston County recorded more than 2,500 truck-related accidents in 2023. Port truck crashes involve multiple liable parties: driver, carrier, chassis leasing company, terminal operator, and cargo shipper. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.

edits.before: Rivers Avenue (US-52) is one of the four deadliest roads in Charleston County and North Charleston's primary commercial corridor. The Rivers Avenue/I-526 interchange produced 62 injuries over a 5-year study period. Heavy truck traffic from port and industrial facilities, Boeing South Carolina, and commercial development create constant hazards. Recent crashes include a cement truck rollover and a tractor-trailer striking the I-526 overhead sign. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.

edits.before: The intersection of Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 is the most dangerous intersection in all of South Carolina, averaging a crash once every three days. High-speed I-26 off-ramp traffic, complex left turns, and heavy commercial truck volume are the primary factors. Common crash types include left-turn collisions, rear-end crashes from sudden stops, T-bone accidents from red-light runners, and pedestrian strikes. South Carolina provides 3 years to file an injury claim (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.
edits.after: A Post and Courier analysis of 2011–2015 collision data recorded 629 crashes at Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 — roughly one every three days, more than at any other intersection in Berkeley, Charleston or Dorchester counties, and second in the state behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia. High-speed I-26 off-ramp traffic, complex left turns, and heavy commercial truck volume are the primary factors. Common crash types include left-turn collisions, rear-end crashes from sudden stops, T-bone accidents from red-light runners, and pedestrian strikes. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.
edits.note: called it the most dangerous intersection in all of South Carolina; the Post and Courier analysis the page body relies on ranked it SECOND statewide, behind I-20 at US-176

edits.before: Abercorn Street between White Bluff Road and DeRenne Avenue is Savannah's most dangerous retail corridor for truck crashes, with the Abercorn & White Bluff intersection ranking as the #1 most dangerous intersection in the city — 1 in 4 crashes results in serious injury or fatality. GDOT data shows a 15–20% increase in accidents over the past five years. Port trucks using Abercorn Extension add heavy commercial volume to a corridor already saturated with driveway conflicts and turning traffic. Georgia gives injury victims 2 years to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and allows recovery if less than 50% at fault. Contact Roden Law's Savannah office at (912) 303-5850 within 24–48 hours to preserve critical evidence.
edits.after: Abercorn Street between White Bluff Road and DeRenne Avenue is one of Savannah's most hazardous retail corridors for truck crashes, with the Abercorn & White Bluff intersection the corridor's worst point. Port trucks using Abercorn Extension add heavy commercial volume to a corridor already saturated with driveway conflicts and turning traffic. Georgia gives injury victims 2 years to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and allows recovery if less than 50% at fault. Contact Roden Law's Savannah office at (912) 303-5850 within 24–48 hours to preserve critical evidence.
edits.note: a '#1 most dangerous intersection' ranking, a '1 in 4 crashes results in serious injury or fatality' ratio, and a '15-20% increase' attributed to GDOT — none traceable to a published source, and the first two were removed from bodies

edits.before: The Aviation Avenue and I-26 interchange in North Charleston is a high-risk truck accident zone adjacent to the I-26/I-526 interchange (354 collisions over 5 years) and Boeing South Carolina. A tractor-trailer carrying an excavator struck the Eagle Drive overpass near mile marker 207 in 2025, shutting down multiple lanes during rush hour. A crash near Aviation Avenue in February 2024 caused an 11-mile backup. Overheight loads, speed-congestion cycles, and Boeing-related industrial truck traffic compound the danger. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.

edits.before: US-17 & SC-544 is the most hazardous intersection in Horry County, with 240 crashes over 3 years (2018-2020). US-17 is the most dangerous road in the county with 2,181 accidents in a single year. Heavy commercial delivery traffic to Surfside Beach tourist businesses shares the intersection with unfamiliar tourists and pedestrians crossing a multi-lane highway. Horry County records over 11,000 crashes per year. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.
edits.after: US-17 & SC-544 is one of the most hazardous intersections in Horry County, with 240 crashes over 3 years (2018–2020). Heavy commercial delivery traffic to Surfside Beach tourist businesses shares the intersection with unfamiliar tourists and pedestrians crossing a multi-lane highway. US-17 carries a disproportionate share of the county's truck traffic along the Grand Strand, which is why crashes cluster on it. South Carolina gives victims 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with recovery if less than 51% at fault.
edits.note: 'US-17 is the most dangerous road in the county with 2,181 accidents in a single year' — removed from bodies in round 2b — plus an unsourced 'over 11,000 crashes per year' county figure

edits.before: Columbia sits at the crossroads of I-20, I-26, and I-77, making its intersections among South Carolina's most dangerous. The I-20/Broad River Road interchange recorded 229 collisions in one year, while "Malfunction Junction" (I-20/I-26) produced 91 crashes including two fatalities. South Carolina's three-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) and modified comparative fault rule (less than 51% at fault) govern how victims recover compensation for injuries caused at these high-risk crossroads.
edits.after: Columbia sits at the crossroads of I-20, I-26, and I-77, and its interchange complexes — particularly the I-20/I-26 junction known as "Malfunction Junction" — handle traffic volumes that exceed their design capacity. South Carolina's three-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) and modified comparative fault rule (less than 51% at fault) govern how victims recover compensation for injuries caused at these high-risk crossroads.
edits.note: the 229-collision and 91-crash single-year counts, both removed from this page's body as untraceable to a stated reporting period

edits.before: The intersection of Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 in North Charleston averages one crash every three days, making it the most dangerous intersection in South Carolina. High-speed off-ramp traffic, complex left turns, and commercial density are the primary factors. Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, injured victims have 3 years to file suit. Government entities like SCDOT may share liability for design deficiencies under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act.
edits.after: A Post and Courier analysis of 2011–2015 collision data recorded 629 crashes at Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 in North Charleston — about one every three days, more than at any other intersection in the tri-county area and second in the state behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia. None of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured. High-speed off-ramp traffic, complex left turns, and commercial density are the primary factors. Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, injured victims have 3 years to file suit. Government entities like SCDOT may share liability for design deficiencies under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act.
edits.note: said the crash frequency makes it the most dangerous intersection in South Carolina; the same page's body says it ranked second statewide and that none of the 629 crashes was fatal
